takeaways: A slab on four edges is one-way only when l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> > 2; then a 1 m strip across the short span is designed as a beam.
Deflection, not bending, often decides slab thickness: check l/d against the basic value times the factor for the steel actually provided.
Two-way moments are α w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>² in both directions; the edge conditions pick the Table 26 row and held-down corners need torsion steel.
Cantilever slabs have their main steel at the top, anchored a full development length beyond the support face.
Continuous slabs use Table 12 and 13 coefficients, which already include pattern loading, with different values for dead and live load.
A stair flight is a one-way slab on its horizontal span; loads go per m² of plan with the slope factor on the waist only.
Flat slabs are designed by the direct design method and are usually decided by punching shear round the columns.
Yield line theory gives an upper bound: the lowest load over all mechanisms is the collapse load.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask one full design: a one-way or two-way slab with given edge conditions, a cantilever slab, or a dog-legged staircase; the types of staircases and an introduction to flat slabs appear as descriptive questions.

bank.q: Explain how a slab supported on four edges shares its load between the two directions. State the IS 456 rules that separate one-way and two-way slabs, and explain how edge conditions, corners and strips enter the design of a two-way slab.
outline: Crossing strips with equal deflection; stiffness ∝ 1/l⁴
Rankine–Grashoff formula with a numerical case
One-way if l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> > 2 or supported on two edges
Table 26 for restrained panels (nine cases), Table 27 for simply supported
M = α w l<sub>x</sub>² in both directions
Middle and edge strips, torsion steel, layer order
answer: Load sharing. Think of the slab as two families of strips, one across each span, crossing at right angles. At each crossing point both strips must deflect the same amount. A simply supported strip under uniform load deflects 5wl⁴/(384EI), so for the same deflection the load each strip takes is inversely proportional to l⁴: the shorter strip is much stiffer and takes most of the load.

answer.text: Rankine–Grashoff. With wx on the short span and wy on the long span:
answer.pre:
w<sub>x</sub> l<sub>x</sub>⁴ = w<sub>y</sub> l<sub>y</sub>⁴,   w<sub>x</sub> + w<sub>y</sub> = w
w<sub>x</sub> = w l<sub>y</sub>⁴/(l<sub>x</sub>⁴ + l<sub>y</sub>⁴),   w<sub>y</sub> = w l<sub>x</sub>⁴/(l<sub>x</sub>⁴ + l<sub>y</sub>⁴)

answer: For l<sub>x</sub> = 4 m and l<sub>y</sub> = 5 m: w<sub>x</sub> = 625/(256 + 625) w = 0.709w and w<sub>y</sub> = 0.291w. For l<sub>y</sub> = 2l<sub>x</sub>: w<sub>x</sub> = 16/17 = 0.941w. So once the long span is twice the short one, the long direction carries only about 6 % of the load.

IS 456 rules. A slab supported on two opposite edges, or on four edges with ly/lx > 2, is designed as one-way: 1 m strips across the short span, with only distribution (minimum) steel along the long span. With ly/lx ≤ 2 it is two-way and is designed by Annex D. Spans are effective spans (cl. 22.2).

Coefficients. The simple split ignores the twisting stiffness of the slab and continuity. IS 456 therefore gives moment coefficients, Mx = αx w lx² and My = αy w lx² (both with lx²). Table 27 applies to simply supported panels whose corners can lift; its values equal the Rankine–Grashoff moments. Table 26 applies to panels whose corners are held down, in nine cases from interior panel to four edges discontinuous; each case has a negative coefficient for the continuous edges and a positive one for mid-span. αx varies with ly/lx; αy is one value per case.

Edge conditions. A continuous edge, where the slab carries on into the next panel, develops a hogging moment and needs top steel; the more edges are continuous, the smaller the mid-span moments. A discontinuous edge is treated as simply supported, with nominal top steel (half the mid-span steel over 0.1l) for partial fixity.

Strips and corners. Each direction is divided into a middle strip (3/4 of the width), which takes the table moments, and two edge strips (1/8 each) with minimum steel. Short-span bars go in the outer layer, so dy = dx − φ. At a corner where both edges are discontinuous, held-down corners need torsion steel in four layers, each 3/4 of the steel for the largest mid-span moment, over lx/5; half of that where one edge is continuous; none where both are continuous.

Summary. The ratio ly/lx decides one-way or two-way; the edge conditions decide the table row; the corners decide the torsion steel; and deflection (lx/D ≤ 28 or 32 for Fe415 when lx ≤ 3.5 m and live load ≤ 3 kN/m², otherwise cl. 23.2) decides the thickness. A neat sketch of a panel with its continuous and discontinuous edges, strips and corner meshes completes the answer.

bank.q: Classify staircases by plan shape and by structural behaviour. Explain how IS 456 fixes the effective span and the loads of a stair flight, with sketches.
outline: Terms: riser, tread, going, waist, landing
Spanning transversely and longitudinally; tread-riser stairs
Load per m² of plan with the slope factor
Depth measured normal to the soffit; detailing at kinks
answer: Terms. Riser R: vertical height of a step. Tread T: horizontal width. Going: horizontal length of a flight. Waist: thickness of the sloping slab, measured at right angles to its soffit. Landing: the level slab at the ends of a flight. A comfortable step keeps 2R + T around 600 mm, for example R = 150 mm and T = 300 mm.

By plan shape. Straight flight (one long run, needs a long hall); quarter-turn (turns 90° at a landing); dog-legged (two parallel flights in opposite directions with no gap between them and a half landing: the most compact and the commonest in houses); open well (a gap between the flights, often for a lift, with a quarter or half landing); bifurcated (one wide flight splitting into two); spiral and helical (round, for small plans or architecture).

By structural behaviour. (1) Spanning transversely: each step spans across the stair, as a cantilever from a wall or a central spine beam, or between two walls or two stringer beams; the waist is thin and the steps carry the load. (2) Spanning longitudinally: the waist slab with the steps on it spans along the slope between landings or beams; the dog-legged and straight flights are usually designed this way. (3) Tread-riser stairs: no waist; each tread and riser act together as a folded plate.

Effective span (cl. 33.1). (a) Flight supported at its top and bottom by beams parallel to the risers: centre-to-centre of the beams. (b) Flight spanning onto the edge of a landing slab that spans parallel to the risers: going + at each end half the landing width or 1 m, whichever is smaller. (c) Landing spanning in the same direction as the flight: flight and landing act as one slab, and the span is centre-to-centre of the supporting beams or walls, measured horizontally. Where spans cross at right angles in an open well, load on the common area is taken half in each direction.

answer.text: Loads. All loads are expressed per m² of plan so that the horizontal span can be used:
answer.pre:
waist  = 25 t √(R² + T²)/T   (slope factor)
steps  = 25 R/2               (triangles)
finish and live load on plan, as given
M<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> l²/8 on the horizontal span l

answer: For R = 160 mm, T = 300 mm and t = 180 mm the slope factor is 1.1333, the waist weighs 25 × 0.18 × 1.1333 = 5.10 kN/m² and the steps 25 × 0.16/2 = 2.00 kN/m².

Detailing. The flight is reinforced like a one-way slab: main bars along the slope at the bottom, distribution bars across. Where the soffit has a re-entrant corner (where a flight meets the landing above it), a bottom bar bent round the corner would pull out through the cover; instead the flight bars run straight on into the top of the landing and the landing bars into the flight, crossing, each with a development length.

answer.text: Sketches. Draw the plan of a dog-legged and an open-well stair, a longitudinal section of a flight showing R, T, the waist and the effective span of case (b), and a cross-section of a cantilever-step stair from a wall.

bank.q: What is a flat slab? Describe its components, the column and middle strips, the conditions and steps of the direct design method, and the punching shear check of IS 456.
outline: Column strip and middle strip widths
answer: Definition. A flat slab is a reinforced concrete slab carried directly on columns, without beams. It gives a flat soffit, lower storey heights, easy formwork and free routing of ducts, so it suits offices, malls, hospitals and car parks. The price is a thicker slab, heavy steel near the columns and the risk of punching shear.

Components. A drop is a thickened part of the slab round the column, rectangular in plan and at least one-third of the panel length in each direction; it adds depth for the hogging moment and shear. A column head (capital) is a flared top of the column; only the part inside a 90° cone or pyramid counts. A slab with neither is a flat plate, used for light loads and short spans. Minimum thickness is 125 mm; the span/d rules apply directly with drops and are multiplied by 0.9 without them.
Strips. The column strip runs along a column line with a width of 0.25l₂ on each side, but not more than 0.25l₁; the middle strip is the rest of the panel. For a 6 m square panel both are 3 m wide.

Conditions of the direct design method (cl. 31.4.1). At least three continuous spans in each direction; rectangular panels with long/short span ≤ 2; successive spans differing by no more than one-third of the longer; columns offset by at most 10 % of the span; live load at most three times the dead load. Otherwise the equivalent frame method is used.

answer.pre:
W  = w<sub>u</sub> l₂ lₙ            (lₙ = clear span ≥ 0.65 l₁)
M₀ = W lₙ / 8
interior span: negative 0.65 M₀, positive 0.35 M₀
column strip: 75 % of negative, 60 % of positive
middle strip: the rest; divide by strip width for kN·m/m

answer: For the 6 m panel of the flat slab chapter, with w<sub>u</sub> = 15.21 kN/m² and lₙ = 5.55 m, M₀ = 351.3 kN·m and the column strip negative moment is 0.75 × 0.65 × 351.3/3.0 = 57.1 kN·m/m. End spans use fractions that depend on the stiffness of the exterior column, and the column strip takes all of the exterior negative moment.

Punching shear (cl. 31.6). The critical section is at d/2 from the face of the column, capital or drop. The shear is the load on the panel outside it, and τv = Vu/(b₀d) must not exceed ks τc with τc = 0.25√fck and ks = 0.5 + βc ≤ 1. Between ks τc and 1.5ks τc shear reinforcement is provided; above that the slab is redesigned. With drops, a second section at d/2 outside the drop is checked.
Sketch. Plan of a panel with columns, drops, column and middle strips and the punching perimeter, and a section through a column showing the drop and the 45° punching cone.

bank.q: Design a simply supported one-way slab for a hall 3.5 m × 9.0 m (clear) on 300 mm walls. Live load 4 kN/m², floor finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415, mild exposure. Sketch the reinforcement.
outline: Deflection check with the Fig. 4 factor
answer: Type. ly/lx = 9.0/3.5 = 2.57 > 2, so the slab is one-way and spans the 3.5 m direction. Design a 1 m strip, b = 1000 mm.

Trial depth. With the Fig. 4 factor near 1.4 for Fe415, l/d ≈ 20 × 1.4 = 28, so d ≈ 3650/28 = 130 mm. With 20 mm cover and 10 mm bars, D = 130 + 25 = 155 mm. Adopt D = 160 mm, d = 160 − 20 − 5 = 135 mm. (A 150 mm slab fails deflection: l/d = 29.0 against 20 × 1.31 = 26.2.)
Effective span. Clear span + d = 3.5 + 0.135 = 3.635 m; centre to centre = 3.5 + 0.30 = 3.80 m. l = 3.635 m.

Moment and shear. Mu = wu l²/8 = 13.50 × 3.635²/8 = 22.30 kN·m/m. Vu = wu l/2 = 13.50 × 3.635/2 = 24.54 kN/m. Mu,lim = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 135² = 50.30 kN·m > Mu, so a singly reinforced under-reinforced section works.
Distribution steel. 192 mm²/m with 8 mm bars: 1000 × 50.27/192 = 262 mm. Provide 8 mm @ 260 mm c/c (≤ 5d and 450 mm), on top of the main bars.

Shear. τv = 24.54 × 10³/(1000 × 135) = 0.182 N/mm². pt = 100 × 524/(1000 × 135) = 0.388 %; Table 19 (M20) by interpolation τc = 0.426 N/mm²; k = 1.28 for D = 160 mm (between 1.30 at 150 and 1.25 at 175), so kτc = 0.545 N/mm² > τv. No shear steel.
Deflection. fs = 0.58 × 415 × 495/524 = 228 N/mm². With pt = 0.39 %, Fig. 4 gives a factor of about 1.42. Allowed l/d = 20 × 1.42 = 28.47; actual l/d = 3635/135 = 26.93. Safe.

answer.text: Detailing. Main bars 10 mm @ 150 mm at the bottom across the 3.5 m span, alternate bars may be bent up or curtailed near the supports (at least half carried into the support); distribution bars 8 mm @ 260 mm along the 9 m length; 20 mm clear cover. Sketch: a plan with the two bar directions and a section through the 3.5 m span showing D = 160 mm, the 300 mm wall bearings and the bars.

answer: Check. Moment capacity with the steel provided: xu = 0.87 × 415 × 524/(0.36 × 20 × 1000) = 26.3 mm, Mu = 0.87 × 415 × 524 × (135 − 0.42 × 26.3) = 23.44 kN·m/m ≥ 22.30. The design is complete.

bank.q: Design an interior panel of a two-way slab, 4.0 m × 5.0 m (effective spans), with corners held down. Live load 3 kN/m², floor finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415, 8 mm bars, 20 mm cover. Show the steel in both directions.
outline: Table 26 coefficients for an interior panel, interpolated
Steel in both directions, layer order, minimum steel
Edge strips; no torsion steel at continuous corners
answer: Type. ly/lx = 5.0/4.0 = 1.25 ≤ 2: two-way. All four edges are continuous (interior panel), so Table 26 case 1 applies.
Depth. The 40 × 0.8 = 32 rule of cl. 24.1 is only for spans up to 3.5 m, so check by cl. 23.2. Try D = 130 mm: dx = 130 − 20 − 4 = 106 mm (short-span bars outer), dy = 106 − 8 = 98 mm.
Loads. Self weight 0.130 × 25 = 3.25; finish 1.00; live 3.00; w = 7.25 kN/m²; wu = 1.5 × 7.25 = 10.875 kN/m². wu lx² = 10.875 × 16 = 174.0 kN.
Coefficients. Interior panel, Table 26: αx(−) is 0.043 at 1.2 and 0.047 at 1.3, so 0.045 at 1.25; αx(+) is 0.032 and 0.036, so 0.034; αy(−) = 0.032 and αy(+) = 0.024 for any ratio.

answer.text: Moments and steel (M = α wu lx²; Ast from the Annex G formula; minimum 0.12 % × 1000 × 130 = 156 mm²/m; spacing ≤ 3d and 300 mm).

answer: All four moments are below M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 98² = 26.5 kN·m, so the sections are under-reinforced. Three of the four are governed by the minimum steel: a 4 m interior panel is lightly stressed.

Detailing. The moments apply to the middle strips (3/4 of each width: 3.0 m and 3.75 m). Edge strips, 0.50 m and 0.625 m wide, get the minimum 156 mm²/m (8 @ 300). Bottom bars run to within 0.25l of the continuous edges; top bars over each beam extend 0.15l into the span, with at least half to 0.3l. All four corners lie between continuous edges, so no torsion steel is needed (Annex D-1.10).
Shear. Safe upper value Vu = wu lx/2 = 21.75 kN/m; τv = 21.75 × 10³/(1000 × 106) = 0.205 N/mm², well below kτc = 1.30 × 0.32 = 0.42 N/mm².

Deflection. Short span, continuous: basic 26. With the mid-span steel pt = 0.158 % and fs = 229 N/mm², the Fig. 4 factor reaches its cap of 2.0. Allowed l/d = 26 × 2.0 = 52; actual 4000/106 = 37.7. Safe.

Check. The short-span mid-span moment 5.92 kN·m/m is 38 % of the Table 27 value for a simply supported panel of the same ratio, 0.0885 × 174.0 = 15.40 (0.084 at 1.2 and 0.093 at 1.3, so 0.0885 at 1.25): continuity and held-down corners have removed most of the sagging moment.

bank.q: Design a cantilever canopy slab projecting 1.5 m clear from a beam, with a roof live load of 0.75 kN/m² and finish 1 kN/m². M20, Fe415, 20 mm cover, 10 mm bars. Show the anchorage of the main bars.
outline: Trial depth from the cantilever span/d of 7
Loads and M<sub>u</sub> at the face
Shear at d from the face
answer: Depth. Basic l/d for a cantilever is 7; with a factor near 1.8 for lightly reinforced slabs, d ≈ 1560/(7 × 1.8) ≈ 124 mm. Adopt D = 150 mm, d = 150 − 20 − 5 = 125 mm. (D = 140 mm fails: l/d = 13.54 against 7 × 2.00 = 14.00.)
Loads. Self weight 0.150 × 25 = 3.75; finish 1.00; live 0.75; w = 5.50 kN/m²; wu = 8.250 kN/m².
Moment at the face. Mu = wu l²/2 = 8.250 × 1.5²/2 = 9.281 kN·m/m (hogging).
Steel. 4.6 Mu/(fck b d²) = 0.1366; Ast = 213 mm²/m, more than the minimum 180 mm²/m. Spacing 1000 × 78.54/213 = 368 mm, limited to 300 mm. Provide 10 mm @ 300 mm c/c at the top (262 mm²/m).
Deflection. Effective span = 1.5 + 125/2000 = 1.5625 m; l/d = 12.50. fs = 0.58 × 415 × 213/262 = 196 N/mm², pt = 0.209 %: the Fig. 4 factor reaches its cap of 2.0. Allowed 7 × 2.0 = 14.0. Safe.
Shear. At d from the face Vu = 8.250 × (1.5 − 0.125) = 11.34 kN/m; τv = 0.091 N/mm² < 1.30 × 0.328 = 0.426 N/mm². Safe.

Anchorage. Ld = φ × 0.87 fy/(4τbd) = 10 × 361.05/(4 × 1.92) = 470 mm. The top bars run at least 470 mm past the face of the beam into the roof slab behind (or are bent down into the beam with an equivalent length), and the beam is designed for the torsion the canopy puts on it.
Distribution steel. 180 mm²/m: 8 mm @ 270 mm c/c parallel to the beam, under the top bars. A few bottom bars (8 mm @ 300) hold the shape and control shrinkage cracks.

Two points decide a cantilever more than its moment does. The first is the deflection check: the basic ratio is only 7, so a canopy that looks thick enough in bending may still fail, as the 140 mm trial did. The second is anchorage and stability: the top bars must be fully developed behind the face, and the supporting beam or the slab behind must hold the canopy down, because the whole moment is carried at one edge with nothing on the free side to help.

answer.text: Check. Capacity with 10 @ 300: xu = 13.1 mm, Mu = 11.29 kN·m/m ≥ 9.28. Sketch: section through beam and canopy with the top bars, their 470 mm anchorage, distribution bars and 20 mm cover.

bank.q: Design a dog-legged staircase for a floor-to-floor height of 3.3 m. Riser 150 mm, tread 280 mm; the landings are 1.0 m wide and span across the stair hall onto walls, parallel to the risers. Live load 3 kN/m², finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415. Sketch the reinforcement of a flight.
outline: Number of risers, treads and the going
answer: Geometry. Risers = 3300/150 = 22, so 11 per flight and 10 treads per flight. Going = 10 × 0.280 = 2.8 m. 2R + T = 580 mm, comfortable. Each flight rises 11 × 0.15 = 1.65 m.
Effective span. The flight spans onto landings that span parallel to the risers, so l = going + at each end the smaller of half the landing width and 1 m = 2.8 + 2 × 0.5 = 3.8 m.
The landing portions are lighter (25 × 0.17 + 4 = 8.25 kN/m²); applying the flight load over the whole span is slightly on the safe side.
Moment. Mu = 16.045 × 3.8²/8 = 28.96 kN·m/m; Vu = 16.045 × 3.8/2 = 30.48 kN/m. Mu,lim = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 144² = 57.2 kN·m. Under-reinforced.
Main steel. 4.6 Mu/(fck b d²) = 0.3212; Ast = 611 mm²/m. 12 mm bars: 1000 × 113.1/611 = 185 mm; provide 12 mm @ 180 mm c/c along the slope (628 mm²/m).
Distribution steel. 0.12 % × 1000 × 170 = 204 mm²/m; 8 mm @ 240 mm c/c across the flight.
Deflection. l/d = 3800/144 = 26.39. fs = 0.58 × 415 × 611/628 = 234 N/mm²; factor ≈ 1.325; allowed 20 × 1.325 = 26.49. Safe, just. (A 160 mm waist fails: 28.36 against 25.28.)

Landings. Each landing is a one-way slab spanning across the hall onto the walls; besides its own weight it carries the end reaction of each flight it supports, 30.48 kN/m (factored) along the flight width, which is added as load on that part of the landing.

answer.text: Detailing. Bottom bars of the flight 12 mm @ 180 along the slope. At the lower kink the soffit is convex and the bars may bend with it into the landing. At the upper kink the soffit has a re-entrant corner, where a bent bar in tension would pull out through the cover; there the flight bars run straight on into the top of the half landing and the landing bars run straight on into the flight, crossing, each with Ld = 564 mm (47φ for 12 mm bars). Distribution 8 mm @ 240.

bank.q: A one-way slab 120 mm thick is continuous over four beams (three equal spans) at 3.2 m centres; the beams are 230 mm wide. Finish 1 kN/m², live load 3 kN/m², M20, Fe415, d = 95 mm. Using IS 456 coefficients, find the design moments and shears and the steel at the critical sections.
outline: Factored dead and live loads separately
Moments at end span, first interior support, interior span
answer: Conditions. Three spans, all equal, uniform load: the coefficients of cl. 22.5 may be used, and the moments may not be redistributed.
Span. Clear span = 3.2 − 0.23 = 2.97 m; 230 mm is less than 1/12 of it (248 mm), so l = smaller of 2.97 + 0.095 and 3.2 = 3.065 m; l² = 9.394 m².
Loads. Dead: 0.12 × 25 + 1.0 = 4.0 kN/m², factored wD = 6.0 kN/m. Live: factored wL = 4.5 kN/m. They are kept apart because Table 12 gives them different coefficients.

answer.text: Moments (Table 12) and steel (Ast from the Annex G formula, minimum 144 mm²/m, spacing ≤ 3d = 285 mm). With three spans the middle span is the interior span and both interior supports are "next to the end support".

answer: Shears (Table 13). End support: (0.4 × 6.0 + 0.45 × 4.5) × 3.065 = 13.56 kN/m. Outer side of the first interior support: (0.6 × 6.0 + 0.6 × 4.5) × 3.065 = 19.31 kN/m; τv = 0.203 N/mm², below 1.30 × τc = 1.30 × 0.405 = 0.527 N/mm² (pt from the top steel there). Safe.
Deflection. End span: l/d = 32.3; with the end-span steel the factor is about 1.51, so the allowed ratio is 26 × 1.51 = 39.4. Safe.

Detailing. Bottom bars in every span, top bars over both interior supports extending at least 0.3l (about 1.0 m) each side, and top bars of half the mid-span steel at the end supports over 0.1l to take the partial fixity of the end beams. Distribution steel 0.12 % × 1000 × 120 = 144 mm²/m: 8 mm @ 340 mm c/c (148 mm²/m), within 5d and 450 mm.

The coefficients already envelope the live-load patterns: the end-span value 1/10 for live load comes from loading the end span and alternate spans, and the support value 1/9 from loading the two spans next to the support. Using them saves drawing several bending moment diagrams, but only for the conditions of cl. 22.5.
Check. The largest moment is −10.33 kN·m/m at the interior supports; it is 1.16 times the end-span sagging moment, which is why the top steel there is the closest spaced.

bank.q: An interior panel of a flat plate floor (no drops) is 5.5 m × 5.5 m on 400 mm square columns, 200 mm thick. Live load 3 kN/m², finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415. Find the column-strip and middle-strip moments by the direct design method, the column-strip steel, and check punching shear and the thickness.
outline: Conditions of the direct design method
Punching at d/2 with k<sub>s</sub> τ<sub>c</sub>
Span/d with the 0.9 factor for no drops
answer: Conditions. Assume at least three spans each way; panels square (ratio 1 ≤ 2); equal spans; columns in line; live load 3 kN/m² ≤ 3 × dead load. The direct design method applies.

answer.text: Distribution. Column strip = 2 × 0.25 × 5.5 = 2.75 m; middle strip 2.75 m.

answer: Column-strip steel (d ≈ 200 − 35 = 165 mm, the mean of the two layers). Negative: Ast = 799 mm²/m, 12 mm @ 140 mm c/c top. Positive: Ast = 323 mm²/m, 10 mm @ 240 mm c/c bottom. Mu,lim = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 165² = 75.1 kN·m > 42.8.

Punching. Perimeter at d/2: side = 400 + 165 = 565 mm, b₀ = 2260 mm. Vu = 13.50 × (5.5² − 0.565²) = 404.1 kN. τv = 404065/(2260 × 165) = 1.084 N/mm². ks = 0.5 + 1 = 1.5, taken as 1; τc = 0.25√20 = 1.118 N/mm². 1.084 < 1.118: safe without shear reinforcement.
For comparison, a 180 mm plate (d = 145 mm) gives τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.21 N/mm² > 1.118: it would need shear reinforcement (allowed up to 1.5 × 1.118 = 1.68 N/mm²) or a drop.

Thickness. No drops, so the basic 26 is multiplied by 0.9. With the column-strip mid-span steel (pt = 0.20 %) the factor is about 1.81: allowed l/d = 26 × 0.9 × 1.81 = 42.4; actual 5500/165 = 33.3. Safe; the slab is also above the 125 mm minimum.

Detailing. Column strips carry top bars over the columns (12 mm @ 140) extending into the span by at least 0.3lₙ, and bottom bars (10 mm @ 240) through the span; middle strips carry lighter top and bottom mesh for 14.3 and 12.3 kN·m/m, not less than the minimum 0.12 % × 1000 × 200 = 240 mm²/m. At least two bottom bars of the column strip in each direction should pass through the column core so that the slab hangs on the column if punching ever starts.
Answer. M₀ = 241.4 kN·m; column strip 42.8 and 18.4 kN·m/m, middle strip 14.3 and 12.3 kN·m/m (negative, positive); punching 1.08 < 1.12 N/mm².

bank.q: A 4.0 m square slab, simply supported on four walls with corners free to lift, carries w<sub>u</sub> = 12 kN/m². Design it by IS 456 Table 27 (d = 100 mm both ways, M20, Fe415), then find its collapse load by yield line theory and comment on the margin.
outline: Moment of resistance m of the steel provided
Yield line pattern and work equation
Collapse load and ratio to w<sub>u</sub>
Lower bound and upper bound methods
answer: Design moment. Table 27 at ly/lx = 1: αx = αy = 0.062. M = 0.062 × 12 × 4.0² = 11.90 kN·m/m in each direction.

Steel. Ast = (0.5 × 20/415)(1 − √(1 − 4.6 × 11.90 × 10⁶/(20 × 1000 × 100²))) × 1000 × 100 = 356 mm²/m. Provide 10 mm @ 220 mm c/c both ways (357 mm²/m). (For simplicity the same d is used both ways; in practice the upper layer has d − φ.)
Mechanism. Isotropic steel and a square slab: yield lines along the two diagonals, four triangular pieces rotating about the walls. Give the centre a deflection δ.

answer.pre:
External work = 4 × w × (L²/4) × δ/3 = w L² δ/3
Internal work  = 4 × m × L × (2δ/L) = 8 m δ
w L² δ/3 = 8 m δ   →   w = 24 m / L²

answer: Collapse load. w = 24 × 11.92/4.0² = 17.88 kN/m², which is 1.49 times the design load 12 kN/m².

Comment. Table 27 takes M = 0.062wL², close to wL²/16 (the Rankine–Grashoff value), while the mechanism needs only m = wL²/24. So a coefficient design has a margin of about 24 × 0.062 = 1.49 on the collapse load, before any extra from rounding the bar spacing: 1.49 here. The coefficient method is a lower bound (it satisfies equilibrium and never asks more than the capacity), while yield line theory is an upper bound; the true collapse load lies between 12 and 17.9 kN/m². Because the corners are free to lift, corner levers form at collapse and lower the yield line load a little, so the real margin is somewhat less than 1.49, but well above 1.

Check of the steel. The capacity of the provided steel, m = 11.92 kN·m/m, almost exactly equals the design moment 11.90 kN·m/m, because 10 mm @ 220 mm gives 357 mm²/m against 356 needed. The collapse load scales with m, so the rounding adds almost nothing here and the whole margin comes from the method itself.

Judgement. The margin is not wasted: it also covers the deflection and cracking that the collapse method ignores. Yield line theory is valuable when a slab is irregular or an existing slab must be checked for a new load, not as a way to cut the steel of a routine panel.

bank.q: A slab 3.6 m × 6.6 m (effective spans), simply supported on walls with corners free to lift, carries w<sub>u</sub> = 10.5 kN/m² (D = 150 mm, d<sub>x</sub> = 125 mm, d<sub>y</sub> = 115 mm, M20, Fe415). A designer treats it as one-way. Compare that design with the two-way design by Table 27 and decide which is right.
answer: Classification. ly/lx = 6.6/3.6 = 1.833 ≤ 2, so IS 456 treats the slab as two-way. The designer's one-way assumption ignores the long-direction bending.
Short span. The one-way moment is 1.09 times the two-way value, so its short-span steel is 10 % more than needed. That is on the safe side.

Long span. The two-way moment 4.67 kN·m/m needs only 115 mm²/m, less than the minimum 180 mm²/m; the one-way design also gives the long direction the minimum (as distribution steel). So the long direction is covered either way here, but only because the slab is near the limit of 2. At ly/lx = 1.3, αy = 0.055 against αx = 0.093: the long-direction moment is then too big for the minimum steel and a one-way design would be unsafe there.

Load sharing check. Rankine–Grashoff: the short span takes 6.6⁴/(3.6⁴ + 6.6⁴) = 91.9 % of the load, so a one-way design ignores about 8 % of the load in the long direction. Table 27 gives αx = 0.1147, close to 0.919/8 = 0.1148, as expected since its values are the Grashoff ones.

Torsion and corners. The corners are free to lift, so no torsion steel is needed in either design; if they were held down (Table 26) the coefficients would be smaller still and torsion steel would be required.

A quick way to see the same result: the share of the load carried along the long span falls as (l<sub>x</sub>/l<sub>y</sub>)⁴. At 3.6 m × 6.6 m it is only about 8 %; at a ratio of 1.3 it would be about a quarter of the load. The code limit of 2 is where this share becomes small enough to be covered by distribution steel.

Verdict. The two-way design is the code design and the more economical one (368 against 404 mm²/m in the short span). The one-way design is safe for this slab only because ly/lx is close to 2; as a method for a panel with ly/lx ≤ 2 it is wrong.

Two parallel flights running in opposite directions with a half landing and no gap between them.
√(R² + T²)/T, converting the sloping waist weight to load per m² of plan.
A slab carried directly on columns without beams.
A thickening of a flat slab round a column, at least one-third of the panel length each way.
A flared top of a column under a flat slab.
In a flat slab, the band 0.25l₂ wide on each side of a column line.
M₀ = W lₙ/8, the total moment of a flat slab panel in one direction.
Shear failure of a slab round a column along a truncated cone or pyramid.
A line along which a slab yields and rotates at a constant moment per metre at collapse.
A load at or above the true collapse load, given by any valid mechanism.
